html:
The Gortyn code is a set of laws carved on a stone wall in Gortyn, a city in southern Crete, in the 5th century BCE, probably around 450 BCE. It is the longest Greek law text that survives.

The inscription has twelve columns of text in the local Dorian dialect. The lines run back and forth, one left to right and the next right to left. The stones were later built into a Roman concert hall, and Italian archaeologists found them in 1884.

The code is mostly about private life:

  • marriage, divorce and the property a wife brings and takes away
  • inheritance, adoption and the marriage of heiresses
  • rape and adultery
  • slaves and serfs, with fines that depend on the status of the people involved

It shows a society very different from Athens, with sharp legal lines between free people, serfs and slaves. It is a rare full look at Greek law outside Athens, set beside earlier codes such as Draco's laws and Solon's reforms and the Roman Twelve Tables of the same years. Crete had been home to Minoan civilisation a thousand years before.
